summary: This document specifies the information in a conceptual database of long-lived cryptographic keys used by many routing protocols for message security. It supports both manual and automated key management and describes the database schema.

plainLanguage.summary: Routers authenticate the routing messages they exchange with a shared secret. This RFC describes a common shape for the table that stores those secrets, so that the tool which manages them does not have to understand each routing protocol separately.

questions: what is the long-lived key database
what fields are in the routing key table
how are routing protocol keys selected
what is a kdf in key table
subtitle: A common table for the long-lived keys that routing protocols use to authenticate their messages.

tldr.problem: Every routing protocol that authenticates its messages needs somewhere to keep long-lived keys, and each one invents its own way of naming and selecting them, so key management software has to know about each protocol.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes a conceptual database, shaped as a table whose rows are keys and whose columns record the name, the peers, the interfaces, the protocol, the derivation function, the algorithm, the key itself and the times it may be used, plus the rules for selecting a row.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard published in April 2014 that has not been obsoleted or updated. It is a conceptual database rather than an implementation, and it registers three IANA registries for the protocol names, derivation functions and algorithms.

facts.label: Key format
facts.value: A lowercase hexadecimal string, most significant octet first

facts.label: KeyTable Protocols registry
facts.value: Specification Required, with no initial registrations

today: RFC 7210 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2014, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It describes a conceptual database rather than a protocol, so what stands behind it is the set of routing protocol specifications that map themselves onto it, and the IANA registries it opened for the protocol names, derivation functions and algorithms.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This document specifies the information that needs to be included in a database of long-lived cryptographic keys in order to key the cryptographic authentication of routing protocols.

The conceptual database is designed to separate protocol-specific aspects from both manual and automated key management. The intent is to allow many different implementation approaches to the specified cryptographic key database, while simplifying specification and heterogeneous deployments. The conceptual database avoids the need to build knowledge of any security protocol into key management protocols. It minimizes protocol-specific knowledge in operational and management interfaces, and it constrains where that knowledge can appear.

Textual conventions are provided for the representation of keys and other identifiers. These conventions should be used when presenting keys and identifiers to operational or management interfaces, or when reading keys and identifiers from those interfaces. This satisfies the operational requirement that all implementations represent the keys and key identifiers in the same way, so that cross-vendor configuration instructions can be provided.

Routing protocols can employ the services of more generic security protocols such as TCP-AO of RFC 5925. Implementations of routing protocols may need to supply keys to databases specific to these security protocols as the associated entries in the conceptual database are manipulated.

In many instances the long-lived keys are not used directly in security protocols, but rather a key derivation function is used to derive short-lived keys from the long-lived key in the database. In other instances, security protocols will directly use the long-lived key from the database. The database design supports both use cases.
sections.plainLanguage: The point is to put the protocol-specific parts in one clearly marked column and keep everything else the same everywhere. Then a tool that loads the table can hand a row to any routing protocol without needing to understand that protocol at all.

sections.title: The Columns of the Key Table
sections.content:
The database is characterized as a table, where each row represents a single long-lived symmetric cryptographic key. Normally each key should have only one row. Only in the rare cases where a key is used for more than one purpose, or where the same key is used with multiple key derivation functions, will multiple rows contain the same key value. The columns represent the key value and attributes of the key. To accommodate manual key management, the format of the fields has been purposefully chosen to allow updates with a plain-text editor and to provide equivalent display on multiple systems.

AdminKeyName holds a human-readable string meant to identify the key for the user, and implementations can use it to uniquely identify rows. The same string can be used on the local system and on peer systems, though that is not required. Routing protocols do not make use of this string; they use the LocalKeyName and the PeerKeyName.

LocalKeyName contains a string identifying the key, used to retrieve the key in the local database when it is received in a message. The protocol defines the form of this field. Many routing protocols restrict their key names to integers that can be represented in 16 or 32 bits. The field typically does not contain data in character sets requiring internationalization, and if a protocol ever needs key names that do, that specification has to address canonicalization and normalization so that key names can be compared using binary comparison.

PeerKeyName is the name of the key used by the local system in an outgoing message. For unicast communication, the PeerKeyName of a key on a system matches the LocalKeyName of the identical key maintained on one or multiple peer systems. For group keys the protocol will typically require this field to be an empty string, as the sending and receiving key names need to be the same.

Peers typically lists the peer systems that have this key in their database. For group keys it names the groups for which the key is appropriate, for example a routing area for a multicast routing protocol. Formally it provides a protocol-specific set of restrictions on the scope in which the key is appropriate.

Interfaces identifies the set of physical and virtual interfaces for which it is appropriate to use the key. When the long-lived value is intended for use on any interface, this field is set to all. The form of these strings is specified by the implementation and is independent of the protocol. Protocols may require support for the field or may indicate that constraining keys by interface is not required. TCP-AO implementations are unlikely to decide which interface to use before key selection, so they are expected to use the same keying material across all interfaces and require the all setting.

Protocol identifies a single routing protocol where this key may be used to provide cryptographic protection. This specification establishes a registry for this field, which also specifies the format of the ProtocolSpecificInfo field for each registered protocol.

ProtocolSpecificInfo contains the protocol-specified information that may be useful for a protocol to apply the key correctly. That information must not be required for a protocol to locate an appropriate key; when a protocol does not need it, the field is required to be empty. Because a row may specify a direction of both, the encoding of this field has to support protocol-specific information for sending and receiving in the same row.

KDF indicates the key derivation function used to generate short-lived keys from the long-lived value. When the value is intended for direct use, the field is set to none. A key derivation function is a one-way function that provides cryptographic separation of key material. It may use inputs from the row and from the message being sent or received, but must not depend on other configuration state.

AlgID indicates which cryptographic algorithm is to be used with the security protocol for the specified peer or peers. It can be an encryption algorithm and mode such as AES-128-CBC, an authentication algorithm such as HMAC-SHA1-96 or AES-128-CMAC, or any other symmetric cryptographic algorithm needed by a security protocol. If the KDF field contains none, the long-lived key is used directly with this algorithm; otherwise the derived short-lived key is used with it. When the long-lived key generates a set of short-lived keys, the AlgID field identifies a ciphersuite rather than a single algorithm.

Key contains the long-lived symmetric cryptographic key as a lowercase hexadecimal string. The size of the key depends on the KDF and the AlgID. For instance, KDF of none with AlgID of AES128 requires a 128-bit key, represented by 32 hexadecimal digits.

Direction indicates whether this key may be used for inbound traffic, outbound traffic, both, or whether it has been disabled and may not currently be used at all. The supported values are in, out, both and disabled.

Four further fields give the times at which the key may be used. SendLifetimeStart and SendLifeTimeEnd give the earliest and latest date and time in Coordinated Universal Time at which the key should be considered for use when sending traffic. AcceptLifeTimeStart and AcceptLifeTimeEnd give the same bounds for processing received traffic. The format in all four is YYYYMMDDHHSSZ, with the Z included as a clear indication that the time is in UTC.
sections.plainLanguage: Each row is one secret key. Alongside the key itself the row records the names the local and peer systems use for it, who may talk to it, which routing protocol it belongs to, how it is turned into a session key, which algorithm it is for, whether it may be used to send, to receive, both or not at all, and the four timestamps that bound its use.

sections.title: Key Selection and Rollover
sections.content:
A protocol may directly consult the key table to find the key to use on an outgoing message. The protocol provides a protocol identifier P and a peer identifier H into the key selection function, and optionally an interface identifier I. Any key that satisfies the following conditions may be selected: the Peers field includes H; the Protocol field matches P; if an interface is specified, the Interfaces field includes I or all; the Direction field is either out or both; and SendLifetimeStart is at or before the current time and the current time is at or before SendLifeTimeEnd.

During key selection there may be multiple entries that simultaneously exist and are associated with different cryptographic algorithms or ciphersuites. Systems should support selection of keys based on algorithm preference, to facilitate algorithm transition.

Multiple entries with overlapping valid periods are expected to be available for orderly key rollover. In these cases the expectation is that systems will transition to the newest key available. To meet that requirement the RFC recommends supplementing the key selection algorithm with the following differentiation: select the long-lived key specifying the most recent time in the SendLifetimeStart field.

To look up a key for validating an incoming message, the protocol provides its protocol P, the peer identifier H, the key identifier L and optionally the interface I. A key is selected if the Peer field includes H; the Protocol field matches P; if the Interface field is provided it includes I or is all; the Direction field is either in or both; the LocalKeyName is L; and AcceptLifeTimeStart is at or before the current time and the current time is at or before AcceptLifeTimeEnd.

Key usage is loosely bound by the times in the AcceptLifeTimeStart and AcceptLifeTimeEnd fields. New security associations should not be established except within the period of use specified by these fields, while allowing some grace time for clock skew. However, if a security association has already been established based on a particular long-lived key, exceeding the lifetime does not have any direct impact. Implementations of security protocols that involve long-lived security associations should be designed to periodically interrogate the database and roll over to new keys without tearing down the security associations.

Rather than consulting the conceptual database, a security protocol such as TCP-AO may update its own tables as keys are added and removed, in which case the protocol needs to maintain its own key information. Some routing protocols use IP Security to provide integrity, and a specification that maps such a routing protocol onto this conceptual database needs to describe how the Security Policy Database is manipulated as rows are added and removed.
sections.plainLanguage: To send, the router looks for a row that matches the peer, the protocol, the interface and the direction, and whose send window covers now. To receive, it does the same and also checks that the key identifier in the message matches. When several rows could match, the newest one wins, which is how keys are replaced without a gap.

sections.title: What a Protocol Specification Must Say
sections.content:
To use the key table database in a protocol specification, a protocol needs to specify certain information. The RFC enumerates the items a protocol must specify.

First, the ways of mapping the information in a key table row to the information needed to produce an outgoing message, stated as an explanation of either how to fill in authentication-related fields in a message based on key table information, or, for protocols such as TCP-AO, how to construct Master Key Tuples or other protocol-specific structures from a key table row. Second, the ways of locating the peer identifier, a member of the Peers set, and the LocalKeyName inside an incoming message. Third, the methods of verifying a message given a key table row, stated directly or in terms of protocol-specific structures such as Master Key Tuples.

Fourth, the form and validation rules for LocalKeyName and PeerKeyName; if either is an integer, the conventions in Section 5.1 are used as a vendor-independent format. Fifth, the form and validation rules for members of the Peers set. Sixth, the algorithms and key derivation functions supported. Seventh, the form of the ProtocolSpecificInfo field. Eighth, the rules for canonicalizing LocalKeyName, PeerKeyName, entries in the Peers set, or ProtocolSpecificInfo, which may include normalizations such as lowercasing hexadecimal strings. Ninth, the indication whether support for the Interfaces field is required by the protocol.

The form of the Interfaces field is not protocol specific but is shared among all protocols on an implementation. If a protocol needs to distinguish instances running over the same interface, that is included in the specification of peers. Generally it is desirable to define the specification of peers so that an operator can use the Interfaces field to refer to all instances of a protocol on a link without having to specify both generic interface information and protocol-specific peer information.
sections.plainLanguage: Each routing protocol that uses the table has to say how to turn a row into the bytes it puts on the wire, how to read the peer and key identifiers out of an incoming message, and how to check the result. Everything else is already fixed by this RFC.

sections.title: Textual Conventions
sections.content:
Key names. When a key for a given protocol is identified by an integer key identifier, the associated key name is represented as lowercase hexadecimal digits with the most significant octet first. The integer is padded with leading zero digits until the width of the key identifier field in the protocol is reached. If a key name contains non-integer human-readable text, its format and encoding may be an issue, particularly when it is used in a protocol between two different types of systems. If characters from the ASCII range are sufficient for a key name, they should be used. If characters outside that range are desirable or required, they must be in an encoding of Unicode.

In the case of an AdminKeyName that uses characters outside of the ASCII range, the AdminKeyName must be encoded using UTF-8 and should be normalized using Unicode Normalization Form KC, to maximize the chance that the strings will compare correctly. However, simply using Unicode Normalization Form KC is not sufficient to account for all issues of string comparison, and the RFC refers to the PRECIS framework for additional information.

Keys. A key is represented as a lowercase hexadecimal string with the most significant octet of the key first. The length of this string depends on the associated algorithm and key derivation function.
sections.plainLanguage: Keys and numeric key names are written the same way everywhere: lowercase hexadecimal, most significant byte first. That way a configuration file written for one vendor can be read by another.

sections.title: Operational Considerations
sections.content: If the valid periods for long-lived keys do not overlap, or the system clocks are inconsistent, it is possible to construct scenarios where systems cannot agree upon a long-lived key. When installing a series of keys to be used one after another, operators should configure the SendLifetimeStart field of a key to be several hours after the AcceptLifeTimeStart field of the key, to guarantee there is some overlap. This overlap is intended to address the clock-skew issue and allow for basic operational considerations. Operators may choose to specify a longer overlap, for example several days, to allow for exceptional circumstances.
sections.plainLanguage: Two routers whose clocks disagree can end up with no key in common. The fix is to start each new key sending a few hours before it starts being accepted, so the two sides overlap even when the clocks are a little off.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Management of encryption and authentication keys has been a significant operational problem, both in terms of key synchronization and key selection. The current guidance of RFC 3562 warns against sharing TCP MD5 keying material between systems and recommends changing keys according to a schedule. The same general operational issues are relevant for the management of other cryptographic keys.

It has been recognized in RFC 4107 that automated key management is not viable in multiple scenarios. The conceptual database specified in this document is designed to accommodate both manual key management and automated key management, and a future specification to automatically populate rows in the database is envisioned.

Designers should recognize the warning provided in RFC 4107: automated key management and manual key management provide very different features. The protocol associated with an automated key management technique will confirm the liveness of the peer, protect against replay, authenticate the source of the short-term session key, associate protocol state information with the short-term session key, and ensure that a fresh short-term session key is generated. An automated key management protocol can also improve interoperability by including negotiation mechanisms for cryptographic algorithms. These valuable features are impossible or extremely cumbersome to accomplish with manual key management.
sections.plainLanguage: The table is a place to put keys, not a way to get them to the other side. The RFC is explicit that the security benefits of an automated key exchange, such as freshness and replay protection, do not come from having a table, and that the table alone cannot deliver them.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The specification defines three registries.

The KeyTable Protocols registry has three columns: a name, a brief description of the ProtocolSpecificInfo, and a reference to a specification defining how the protocol is used with the key table. All assignments are made on a Specification Required basis. Each registration entry must contain the protocol name, unique within the registry, the protocol-specific info and the reference. The specification needs to describe the parameters required for using the conceptual database, which typically means it focuses more on the application of security protocols with the key tables than on being a new security protocol specification. There are no initial registrations.

The KeyTable KDFs registry also has three columns, and all assignments are made on a First Come First Served basis. The initial contents of this registry and of the AlgIDs registry are chosen based on the algorithms defined for TCP-AO. The initial entries are none for no key derivation function, AES-128-CMAC for AES-CMAC using 128-bit keys, and HMAC-SHA-1 for HMAC using the SHA-1 hash.

The KeyTable AlgIDs registry has the same three columns and the same assignment policy. Its initial entries are AES-128-CMAC for AES-CMAC using 128-bit keys, AES-128-CMAC-96 for AES-128-CMAC truncated to 96 bits, and HMAC-SHA-1-96 for HMAC SHA-1 truncated to 96 bits.
sections.plainLanguage: Three lists are set up for IANA to maintain: the routing protocols that can use the table, the derivation functions they allow, and the algorithms they allow. The last two start with the ones already used by the TCP authentication option.

viz.caption: The columns of the key table

cells: AdminKeyName
A human-readable string to identify the key for the user. Routing protocols do not use it.
LocalKeyName
The name the local system uses, used to retrieve the key when it is named in an incoming message.
PeerKeyName
The name the local system uses for the key in an outgoing message.
Peers
The peer systems that hold this key, or for group keys the groups for which it is appropriate.
Interfaces
The interfaces for which the key is appropriate, or "all".
Protocol
The single routing protocol where this key may be used.
ProtocolSpecificInfo
Information useful for applying the key correctly. It must never be needed to locate a key.
KDF
The key derivation function used to generate short-lived keys, or "none" for direct use.
AlgID
The cryptographic algorithm used with the security protocol.
Key
The long-lived symmetric key, as a lowercase hexadecimal string.
Direction
Whether the key may be used inbound, outbound, both, or is disabled.
Send and Accept lifetimes
Four timestamps in YYYYMMDDHHSSZ giving when the key may be used for sending and for accepting.

items.title: Outgoing message
items.text: The peer, the protocol, the interface and the direction must match, and the current time must fall inside the send lifetime.

items.title: Incoming message
items.text: The same checks, plus the LocalKeyName must match the key identifier in the message, and the time must fall inside the accept lifetime.

items.title: Rollover
items.text: Where several rows are valid at once, the one with the most recent SendLifetimeStart is chosen.

items.title: Algorithm preference
items.text: Systems should support selecting a key by algorithm preference, to make a move to a new algorithm easier.

items.label: No KDF
items.desc: No key derivation function is used with this key, so the long-lived key is used directly.

items.label: AES-CMAC with 128-bit keys
items.desc: The key derivation function uses AES-CMAC with 128-bit keys.

items.label: HMAC with SHA-1
items.desc: The key derivation function uses HMAC with the SHA-1 hash.
